introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 4 b) : les valeurs mondiales (croissance d'environ 1 % par an, fécondité d'environ 2,3, 8 milliards en 2022, pic vers les années 2080 autour de 10 milliards) sont les ordres de grandeur des projections des Nations unies ; la croissance du Cameroun (environ 2,5 % par an) et sa fécondité (4 à 5 enfants) sont des ordres de grandeur. La baisse démographique de la Chine est mentionnée sans chiffre. À faire relire.

Question 4 a) : les exemples (politique de l'enfant unique en Chine de 1979 à 2015, planification familiale de l'Inde depuis les années 1950, Thaïlande, Kenya, Singapour) sont reconnus ; l'existence de services de planification familiale dans les centres de santé du Cameroun est donnée de façon générale.

Question 4 c) : densités « parmi les plus élevées du Cameroun », températures et pluies de la région (environ 18 à 22 degrés ; 1 500 à 2 500 mm) données en ordres de grandeur ; mention de l'absence de la mouche tsé-tsé dans les hautes terres (élevage du Nord-Ouest) à relire.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about » ou « more than ». Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) de trois sous-questions : codées « a », « b », « c » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b », « OR-c » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou`.

Sujet scanné de cinq pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions, une page de planche de carte topographique 1:50 000 « Dufftown » avec ses signes conventionnels, puis le fond de carte du Cameroun pour la question 3c i). Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2024, Three Hours. Filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés. La planche topographique (page 4) appartient aux épreuves de cartographie (Paper 3) et ne sert à aucune question de ce Paper 2 : non transcrite. Seul le fond de carte du Cameroun (page 5) est utilisé (question 3).

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 8+8+9, Q2 6+10+9, Q3 8+8+(3+6=9), Q4 6+10+9, Q5 5+9+11, Q6 8+9+8, Q7 EITHER 9+8+8, OR 6+10+9). Aucun écart avec le sujet. Le sujet imprime des marks pour un ensemble de sous-points (ex. Q1 a (i)+(ii) = 8 marks) : le corrigé les regroupe sous une seule sous-question.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) For countries with expansive population pyramids, discuss **THREE** measures adopted to check rapid population growth.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
An **expansive population pyramid** (a wide base, narrowing quickly upwards) shows a high birth rate, a large proportion of young people and rapid growth (for example Nigeria, Niger, Cameroon, Uganda). Measures to slow the growth are of three main kinds (2 marks each).

**1. Family planning and health education.** Governments and NGOs provide free or cheap **contraceptives, advice and clinics**, and campaigns on small families and child spacing. In India a national family-planning programme has operated since the 1950s; in Thailand a community-based programme and in Kenya a national programme helped to bring down fertility; in Cameroon family-planning services are offered in health centres. A reduction in **infant mortality** (vaccination, clean water, better care) is also important, because parents who are sure that their children will survive choose to have fewer.

**2. Education and employment of women, and a later age at marriage.** Girls who stay at school and women who have jobs marry later, have fewer children and make more use of family planning. Laws that raise the minimum age at marriage and ban early and forced marriage have the same effect, and so does the improvement of the status of women (access to credit and land).

**3. Legislation, incentives and disincentives.** Some governments use laws or economic rewards. China's **one-child policy (1979 to 2015)** limited births with fines and benefits, and was later relaxed to two and then three children; India and other countries have used tax or housing incentives and sometimes limits on benefits for large families; in Singapore small families were encouraged by tax and school-priority measures. (These coercive methods raise ethical questions, and the success is greater when the policy is accepted voluntarily.)

(Other measures: promotion of emigration, and urbanisation and economic development, which lower fertility.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Using **TWO** arguments, how far do you agree with the assertion that the global population problem is no longer one of rapid population growth but is one of population decline.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The assertion says that the world's main demographic problem has changed from fast growth to decline. It is **partly true**: growth has slowed worldwide and many countries are shrinking, but the world's population is **still growing**, and fast in some regions. Two arguments are given for each side (5 marks for each, with a reasoned conclusion).

**Argument 1: the evidence of decline and of the end of rapid growth (agree).**
- The world growth rate has fallen from a peak of about 2 per cent per year in the late 1960s to about 1 per cent today, and the average number of children per woman has fallen to about 2.3 (close to the replacement level of about 2.1). The United Nations projects that the world's population will **peak this century (probably in the 2080s) at about 10 billion**, and then decline.
- A growing number of countries already have **fertility below replacement and shrinking populations**: Japan, South Korea, Italy, Germany, Russia and the countries of Eastern Europe, and China, which has recently begun to lose population. The problems are those of **population decline and ageing**: a shrinking workforce, a high dependency ratio, a heavy burden of pensions and health care, abandoned rural areas and the closure of schools, and the need for immigration or higher productivity.

**Argument 2: rapid growth is still the problem in many places (disagree).**
- The world's population passed **8 billion in 2022** and still increases by about 70 to 80 million a year. The growth is concentrated in **sub-Saharan Africa**, where many countries (including Cameroon, with growth of about 2.5 per cent a year) have fertility rates of about 4 to 5 children per woman and expansive pyramids; their populations double in about 25 to 30 years, which puts pressure on food, water, jobs, housing, schools and services, and leads to rapid urbanisation, deforestation and poverty.
- Because of **population momentum** (a large young generation entering the reproductive years), the population will continue to rise for decades even if fertility falls to replacement level; the decline predicted is for the second half of the century and not yet.

**Conclusion.** To a **limited extent** I agree: the *global rate* of growth has slowed and decline is a real problem for rich and for East Asian and European countries; but the assertion is too sweeping, since the world is still adding people and the problem is **unequal**: rapid growth in the poorest regions and decline and ageing in the richest. The population problem is therefore not one problem but a **regional difference** in demographic trends.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Examine **THREE** physical factors that have influenced the distribution of population in the Western Highlands of Cameroon.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Western Highlands (the West, North-West and parts of the South-West regions) have some of the **highest rural population densities in Cameroon**, especially in the Bamileke plateau and the Bamenda and Bamoun areas, although the population is unevenly spread. Three physical factors are examined (3 marks each).

**1. Fertile volcanic soils.** The lava, ash and basalt of the Cameroon Volcanic Line weather quickly to give deep, dark, fertile **volcanic soils** that are rich in minerals; they support intensive food-crop farming (maize, beans, cocoyams, Irish potatoes, vegetables) and cash crops (arabica coffee, tea, bananas and plantains, and on the slopes of Mount Cameroon, plantations). They can carry a dense farming population, whereas where the soil is thin, rocky or leached (the steep upper slopes, and the poor granitic areas) densities are low. The soils of the Mount Cameroon slopes attracted plantations and settlers.

**2. Climate and altitude.** Altitude moderates the heat, so that the highlands (about 1,000 to 2,000 m) have a **cool, healthy climate** (mean temperatures about 18 to 22 degrees Celsius), with a reliable annual rainfall (about 1,500 to 2,500 mm) with a long wet season, which allows two crop seasons. The cool climate is also free of the **tsetse fly** and has less malaria than the hot lowlands, which allows the keeping of cattle and a healthier population; this explains the concentration of people. At the highest altitudes (above about 2,500 m on Oku, Bamboutos and Mount Cameroon) it is too cold, wet and exposed, and population density falls.

**3. Relief and drainage.** Gently sloping plateaus, flat valley floors and plains (such as the Ndop plain) are suitable for farming, building and communications, and they have attracted **dense settlement**, with many streams and springs which give water for people and farms. The **steep slopes, deep gorges and rugged mountains** are difficult to farm and to reach and are subject to erosion and landslides, and so have fewer people; people use terracing and ridges to farm the slopes where land is short. The mountains also gave **defence** in the past (the Bamileke chiefdoms), but this is a human factor.

**Conclusion:** the fertile volcanic soils and the moderate, reliable climate are the main attractions; relief both helps (plateaus, basins) and hinders (steep, high land). Human factors (the history of the chiefdoms, cash crops, roads and towns) have also influenced the distribution.
